extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, judges, and advanced law students studying equity practice in patent litigation
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and standards governing pleadings (joinder, demurrer, pleas, answers), defenses (laches, estoppel, licensee rights), and procedural practice in equity suits on patents. Focus is on what must be alleged, when particular defenses are appropriate, and how courts treat timing and form of pleadings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joinder of multiple patents in one bill
rubrics_metrics.description: The fact that the inventions are capable of a joint employment, and that the defendant has thus wrongfully employed them, entitles the plaintiff to regard this wrongful use as constituting a single injury, and to seek his redress for it in a single action, although the defences to each patent may be different and unconnected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The bill must aver, and the evidence must prove, the joint employment of the several inventions. If inventions are incapable of a united use, or are applied to separate uses by the defendant, the infringements are distinct and a bill counting upon more than one of them is multifarious. A bill is not rendered multifarious when all patents are alleged to be infringed by one machine. Courts encourage single suits on a number of patents to avoid multiplicity of actions but require allegations/proof of conjoint use. (Cases: Consolidated Electric Light Co. v. Brush Co.; Shickle v. South St. Louis Foundry Co.; Nourse v. Allen.)

rubrics_metrics.name: When a bill alleging many patents is multifarious
rubrics_metrics.description: A bill will be multifarious when it charges separate infringements of different patents or infringements by different defendants, or when inventions cannot be unitably used or are separately used by defendant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multifariousness arises where the inventions are incapable of united use or are applied to separate machines/uses. One bill cannot embrace infringements of two wholly separate patents for non-unitable inventions. By contrast, alleging infringement of several claims of the same patent or several patents all infringed by one machine may avoid multifariousness. (Cases: Hayes v. Dayton; Nourse v. Allen; Deering v. Winona Harvester Works.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to aver joint use when suing several patents
rubrics_metrics.description: A bill alleging the infringement of several patents must aver that the inventions are capable of joint use and are so used by the defendant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the complaint fails to allege joint use where necessary, it may be demurrable as multifarious. Alleging all patents infringed by a single machine can suffice to avoid multifariousness, but the plaintiff still must plead and later prove the joint employment. (Cases: Kaolatype Engraving Co. v. Hoke; Barney v. Peck.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of general demurrer in equity
rubrics_metrics.description: A general demurrer to a bill attacks defects apparent on the face of the bill — jurisdictional defects, capacity of parties, or want of proper allegations in the bill itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Objections as to form must be taken by demurrer; after evidence is given the bill will not be studied to discover defects. If averments show patent not patentable, patent invalid, lack of plaintiff's interest, distinct infringements, different defendants, or adequate remedy at law, demurrer may be sustained and the bill amended or dismissed. (Cases: McCoy v. Nelson; Pelham v. Edelmeyer.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability and demurrer
rubrics_metrics.description: The question of patentability cannot be decided on demurrer except in clear cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A demurrer denying the invention is patentable does not necessarily admit patentability; courts will decide patentability on demurrer only when the invalidity is apparent on the face of the bill. (Cases: Blessing v. Steam Copper Works; Dick v. Oil Well Supply Co.; Kaolatype Engraving Co. v. Hoke.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Variance between original patent and re-issue on demurrer
rubrics_metrics.description: A variance between the original and the re-issue cannot be taken advantage of on demurrer unless the original is set out in the complaint or attached to it, or profert is made of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Issues arising from departures of a re-issue from its original are often procedural and require the original patent to be before the court to be raised by demurrer. Delay in applying for re-issue (laches) is a question of law for the court and may be raised by demurrer if apparent. (Cases: Adams v. Westlake Mfg. Co.; Wollensak v. Reiher.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Demurring to part of the bill; pleading and answering
rubrics_metrics.description: A defendant may demur to one part of the bill, plead to another part, and answer the remainder, but he is not permitted to demur, plead, and answer to the entire bill at once, especially when the answer contains all the objections urged by the demurrer or the plea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a demurrer and answer are filed simultaneously the plaintiff may waive some objections if he goes to argument on the demurrer. Where a demurrer objects to the whole bill and part only, the court may dismiss as to the defective part and require answer as to the residue. Failure to demur in proper time operates as waiver of defects not ipso facto destructive. (Cases: Adams v. Howard; Hayes v. Dayton.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature and proper use of a plea in equity
rubrics_metrics.description: A plea in equity is a special answer urging some particular defence (jurisdictional facts, statute, record, or other matter) which reduces the issue to a single point; it must not, except in special cases, anticipate the answer by denying substantial allegations of the bill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General defences not averring new matter cannot be made under a special plea. The plea may be used to raise matters not apparent on the face of the bill (e.g., expiration of the patent before suit) and may displace the equity of the bill if it states new matter. But issues of infringement and most issues on the merits must be raised by answer, not plea. (Cases: Story Eq. PL §§ 647–837; Hubbell v. De Land.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal requirements for a plea: single, clear, unevasive
rubrics_metrics.description: A plea in equity must be single, clear, and unevasive; it may cover several facts when together they constitute one defence, but if it embraces several defences it is fatally defective for duplicity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Double pleading in equity is not permitted except by special leave of the court; where a defendant files several pleas without leave, he may be ordered to elect or have pleas treated as an answer. A plea denying infringement only will be struck out on motion since the same matter should be set up in the answer. (Cases: Giant Powder Co. v. Safety Nitro-Powder Co.; Reissner v. Anness.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of setting down or joining issue on a plea
rubrics_metrics.description: By setting down the plea for argument the plaintiff admits the truth of its averments; by joining issue he admits its sufficiency as a defence; if the plea's allegations are sustained the bill must be dismissed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A replication to a plea admits its form and substance, and long neglect to join issue may operate as admission. If plea overruled defendant may file an answer or submit to decree. Affidavits introduced without notice or opportunity to cross-examine are inadmissible on plea. (Cases: Goodyear v. Toby; Bean v. Clark.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and special significance of answers in equity
rubrics_metrics.description: An answer in equity is a denial, or a confession and avoidance, of the material allegations in the bill and is the method by which the defendant sets forth his general defences; in equity, defenses available at law may be resorted to, and certain defenses (estoppel, laches, equitable rights) have especial significance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A licensee treated as an infringer may defend on any ground open to infringers regardless of covenants in his license; laches and acquiescence can defeat equitable relief such as injunctions even where legal relief might still be available. Delays excused by bankruptcy, other suits, or lack of notice may avoid laches. (Cases: Kittle v. Hall; McLaughlin v. People's Railway Co.; Pelham v. Edelmeyer.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Laches and delay as defenses in equity
rubrics_metrics.description: Laches (unreasonable delay in enforcing rights) is a good defense in equity and may bar injunctions or past profits depending on circumstances; whether delay in applying for re-issue is reasonable is a question of law for the court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A delay of many years (e.g., thirteen) may prevent an injunction though damages might still be recoverable. Seasonable notice to infringer followed by suit within reasonable time rebuts laches. Delay pending other suits is not laches. An assignee of past-infringement claims may be barred by the assignor's laches. Laches apparent on the face of the bill may be raised by demurrer. (Cases: McLaughlin v. People's Railway Co.; New York Grape Sugar Co. v. Buffalo Grape Sugar Co.; Kittle v. Hall.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Estoppel, acquiescence, and innocent use
rubrics_metrics.description: Equity favors estoppel as a defense: laches, acquiescence or misleading conduct by the patentee may bar equitable relief; but if the defendant acted in good faith and the patentee had no reasonable opportunity to prevent appropriation, estoppel may not apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where defendants innocently used the invention believing they might rightfully do so, and the patentee was powerless or passive, courts may refuse to estop the patentee. If defendants knowingly appropriated what they did not own, equity will not shield them. (Cases and discussion: McMullin v. Barclay; Ryan v. Goodyear.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of the answer: joinder and specificity of defenses
rubrics_metrics.description: The answer must include all matters of defence the defendant intends to rely on (except those proper for plea or demurrer); any number of defenses may be joined if consistent; inconsistent defences create repugnancy and are fatal unless cured.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each defence must be distinctly and affirmatively stated with particularity as to time, place, person, and circumstances so plaintiff knows the precise attack. The answer must apprise the plaintiff of the defendant's theory as to scope and meaning of the patent; defendant cannot set up hypothetical defenses based on possible future constructions by the court. Defences not raised in the answer will generally be considered waived. (Cases: Sessions v. Romadka; Graham v. Mason; National Mfg. Co. v. Meyers.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Particularity required for affirmative defenses (e.g., prior use/prior knowledge)
rubrics_metrics.description: Affirmative defenses, especially prior knowledge or prior use, must be alleged with particularity (time, place, person) and proved accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substantial matters of defence as to novelty must be set up in the answer with sufficient particularity that the plaintiff may know what he has to meet. Failure to plead these specifics may forfeit the defense. (Cases: Searls v. Bouton; Brown v. Hall.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of failing to set up defenses in the answer
rubrics_metrics.description: Defenses not inserted in the answer will not be considered by the court; long neglect to join issue on a plea may admit its truth and sufficiency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A general defence of 'want of equity' is insufficient; material facts forming the foundation for evidence must be laid in the pleadings. Where the answer is defective it may be amended. (Cases: Bates v. Coe; Puett v. Bransford; Doughty v. West.)
